docs.title: Analysis Support Hub
docs.text:
Welcome to the Analysis Support Hub.

This resource is designed to help you overcome common challenges that may appear while working with information, evidence, observations, findings, and conclusions.

The hub is organized around problems rather than methods. Instead of searching for a specific technique, start by identifying the challenge you are currently facing. Each problem page includes:

  • Common situations where the problem may occur.
  • Self-reflection questions to help diagnose the issue.
  • Possible approaches that may help address the problem.
  • Supporting frameworks, techniques, and tools for further exploration.

docs.title: How to Get Started?
docs.text:
1. Open the Quick Problem Finder.
  2. Identify the situation that most closely matches your current challenge.
  3. Review the self-reflection questions.
  4. Explore the suggested approaches, frameworks, techniques, and tools.
  5. Apply the ideas that best fit your project and continue your analysis.

This hub is intended as a practical reference. You do not need to read it from beginning to end. Use it whenever you encounter a challenge during your analysis process.

To learn more about the purpose and scope of this resource, visit the About page

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Provide a practical support resource that helps students identify, understand, and overcome common analysis challenges.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: This site is optimized for students enrolled in PS5006 (Social Media and Information Technology) who are developing Analysis & Information projects. However, any student working with information, evidence, observations, findings, and conclusions may benefit from the approaches, frameworks, techniques, and tools presented throughout this hub.

docs.title: What This Hub Is
docs.text:
This hub is a practical reference designed to support students during the analysis process.

Rather than teaching a single method, framework, or software tool, the hub helps students identify common analysis challenges and explore possible ways to address them.

Each section focuses on a specific problem that may arise while working with information, evidence, observations, findings, and conclusions.

docs.title: What This Hub Is Not
docs.text:
This hub is not a step-by-step analysis course.

It is not intended to replace classroom instruction, project requirements, or teacher feedback.

The approaches, frameworks, techniques, and tools presented throughout the hub are not mandatory procedures. They are possible options that may help address specific challenges.

There is rarely a single correct way to approach an analysis problem. Different projects may require different methods, perspectives, and solutions.

docs.title: AI Use
docs.text:
The approaches, frameworks, techniques, and tools presented in this hub may be applied independently or with the support of AI systems.

When using AI, students remain responsible for evaluating information, validating results, reviewing assumptions, and making final decisions about their work.

AI can support analysis, but it should not replace critical thinking, evidence evaluation, or professional judgment.

docs.title: How To Use This Hub
docs.text:
When you encounter a challenge:

  1. Identify the problem that most closely matches your situation.
  2. Review the self-reflection questions.
  3. Explore the suggested approaches.
  4. Consider the supporting frameworks, techniques, and tools.
  5. Apply the ideas that are most useful for your project.

Use this hub as a practical reference throughout your analysis process rather than reading it sequentially from beginning to end.

docs.title: 1. My Information is Incomplete, Inconsistent, or Unreliable
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Different files or records contain conflicting information.
  • Key information is missing from the available records.
  • You suspect errors or inconsistencies in the available information.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Are important data or records missing?
  • Can the information be verified?
  • What information appears incomplete?
  • What information appears inconsistent?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Data Cleaning. Review and improve the quality of available information by identifying errors, duplicates, inconsistencies, and missing information.
  • Data Quality Review. Evaluate whether the available information is complete, consistent, accurate, and appropriate for the project.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Completeness Review
  • Consistency Review
  • Cross-Checking
  • Data Audit Checklist
  • Duplicate Identification
  • Error Correction
Possible Tools
  • Advanced Data Cleaning & Wrangling Tools (OpenRefine)
  • Data Validation Tools
  • Database & Data Management Tools
  • Electronic Worksheets (Excel, Google Sheets)
Online Sources
  • IBM: Data Quality Overview — An industry standard explaining how missing, inconsistent, or duplicate data impacts analysis outcomes.
  • Purdue University (Purdue OWL): Evaluating Sources of Information — An academic framework to evaluate source credibility and handle conflicting data points.
  • Stony Brook University: Data Cleaning and Wrangling — A practical guide on identifying anomalies, structural errors, and utilizing data-cleaning tools.

docs.title: 10. I Do Not Understand Why This May Be Happening
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• A pattern exists, but the reasons behind it are uncertain.
  • An observation or finding has been identified, but its causes remain unclear.
  • Multiple factors may be contributing to the same result.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Are there alternative explanations?
  • What factors may contribute to this result?
  • What possible causes should be considered?
  • Which causes appear most consistent with the evidence?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Comparative Analysis. Compare groups, conditions, categories, or situations to identify factors associated with an observed result.
  • Alternative Explanation Analysis. Generate and evaluate multiple possible causes before selecting the most plausible explanation.
  • Root Cause Analysis. Investigate underlying causes that may contribute to an observed result.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • 5 Whys
  • Alternative Cause Exploration
  • Cause-and-Effect Mapping
  • Ishikawa Diagram
  • Root Cause Tree
  • Systems Thinking
Possible Tools
  • AI Root-Cause Prompting Systems
  • Diagramming Tools
  • Mind-Mapping Tools
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 11. I Have Many Findings and Do Not Know Which Matter Most
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Multiple findings appear relevant.
  • Several findings have been developed from the analysis.
  • You are unsure which findings deserve greater attention.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Which findings contribute most to understanding the project?
  • Which findings deserve communication or further development?
  • Which findings are most relevant to the project objective or question?
  • Which findings are supported by the strongest evidence?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Impact Assessment. Evaluate how much each finding contributes to understanding the project, answering the project question, or explaining the observed results.
  • Prioritization. Determine which findings deserve greater attention based on relevance, evidence strength, impact, or significance.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Criteria-Based Ranking
  • Impact Analysis
  • Pareto Analysis
  • Significance Comparison
  • So-What? Framework
Possible Tools
  • Digital Kanban & Prioritization Boards (Trello, Notion)
  • Qualitative Coding & Analysis Tools (Taguette, Atlas.ti)
  • Mind-Mapping Tools
  • Claim-Evidence Matrix Tools (for weight-of-evidence assessment)
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 12. I Am Not Sure What Conclusions Can Reasonably Be Supported
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Findings have been developed, but conclusions remain uncertain.
  • Several conclusions seem possible.
  • You are concerned about making claims that exceed the available evidence.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Are important limitations being considered?
  • Does the conclusion go beyond what the evidence supports?
  • Does the conclusion remain faithful to the findings?
  • Which findings support this conclusion?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Conclusion Validation. Determine whether conclusions remain consistent with the findings and evidence developed during analysis.
  • Scope and Limitation Review. Evaluate whether conclusions remain within the boundaries and limitations of the project.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Boundary Checking
  • Conclusion Validation Checklist
  • Finding-to-Conclusion Mapping
  • Limitation Analysis
  • Scope Review
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Academic Search Engines (Elicit, Consensus)
  • Annotation & Evidence Tracking Tools
  • Claim-Evidence Matrix Tools (Notion, Airtable, Structured Tables)
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 13. I Do Not Know When Analysis Is Sufficient
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Additional analysis continues to generate similar findings.
  • New analysis produces little additional insight.
  • You are uncertain whether further analysis will add meaningful value.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Am I continuing analysis without a clear purpose?
  • Do the findings adequately explain the observations?
  • Have I answered the project question or objective?
  • Would additional analysis likely produce meaningful new insights?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Prioritization. Focus attention on the most meaningful findings rather than continuing unnecessary analysis.
  • Project Alignment Review. Evaluate whether the analysis adequately addresses the project's objective, question, or purpose.
  • Scope and Limitation Review. Determine whether additional analysis would meaningfully improve understanding of the project.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Finding Prioritization
  • Law of Diminishing Returns Checklist
  • Objective Alignment
  • Research Question Alignment
  • Timeboxing & Scope-Creep Constraints
Possible Tools
  • Checklist & Progress Tracking Tools
  • Scope Management & Project Tracking Tools (Notion, Trello, Asana)
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Information is scattered across multiple files, documents, or sources.
  • Large amounts of information feel overwhelming.
  • Multiple files contain similar information.
  • You are unsure where to begin reviewing the information.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Can the information be filtered?
  • Can the information be grouped?
  • Do I need to review all available information?
  • Which information is most relevant to the project?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Information Organization. Organize information into structures that make it easier to review, understand, compare, and analyze.
  • Information Reduction. Reduce the amount of information being reviewed by focusing on the most relevant, representative, or useful information.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Categorization
  • Filtering
  • Grouping
  • Representative Sampling
  • Sorting
  • Tagging
Possible Tools
  • Annotation & Note-Taking Tools
  • Qualitative Coding & Analysis Tools (Taguette, Atlas.ti)
  • Electronic Worksheets (for quantitative data pooling)
  • Mind-Mapping Tools
Online Sources
  • Stony Brook University: Data Cleaning and Wrangling - Useful for understanding how to group, sort, and handle high-volume datasets systematically.

docs.title: 3. I Am Not Sure What Information Matters
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Large amounts of information appear potentially relevant.
  • You are unsure which information is most relevant to the project.
  • You cannot determine which information deserves further analysis.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Which information appears most relevant?
  • Which information can be set aside?
  • Which information directly supports the project objective?
  • Which information helps answer the project question?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Prioritization. Determine which information deserves greater attention based on its importance, usefulness, relevance, or analytical value.
  • Relevance Assessment. Evaluate whether information directly supports the project's objective, question, observations, findings, or conclusions.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Criteria Definition
  • Evidence Selection
  • Highlighting and Annotation
  • Information Ranking
  • Priority Matrix
  • Relevance Screening
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Academic Search & Evidence Discovery Tools (Elicit, Consensus)
  • Annotation & Note-Taking Tools
  • Reference Management Tools with Tagging Systems (Zotero, Mendeley)
Online Sources
  • Purdue OWL: Evaluating Sources
  • UNC Writing Center: Evidence

docs.title: This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Information appears random or disconnected.
  • Large datasets make it difficult to notice trends.
  • You have reviewed the information several times but no meaningful patterns emerge.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Do any trends, similarities, or differences appear repeatedly?
  • Have I compared groups, categories, or time periods?
  • Have I organized the information in different ways?
  • What information appears most frequently?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Comparative Analysis. Compare groups, categories, conditions, or time periods to identify similarities, differences, and trends.
  • Pattern Exploration. Search for recurring characteristics, frequencies, trends, clusters, or regularities within the information.
  • Visual Analysis. Represent information visually to make patterns, concentrations, differences, and trends easier to recognize.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Frequency Analysis
  • Group Comparisons
  • Pareto Analysis
  • Segmentation
  • Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke)
  • Trend Analysis
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Data Analysis Assistants & Code Interpreters (Julius AI, Claude Artifacts, ChatGPT Data Analysis)
  • Data Visualization Tools
  • Electronic Worksheets (specifically for Pivot Tables & Data Sorting)
  • Qualitative Thematic Mapping Tools
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 5. I Cannot Identify Relationships Between Variables, Categories, or Observations
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Information contains multiple categories or factors that may interact.
  • Patterns appear to exist, but connections are unclear.
  • Variables seem related, but the relationship cannot be explained.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Are there relationships that appear consistently across the information?
  • Do similar observations share common characteristics?
  • What changes when another variable changes?
  • Which variables or categories may be connected?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Comparative Analysis. Compare categories, groups, conditions, or time periods to identify possible relationships and connections.
  • Relationship Exploration. Investigate whether variables, categories, observations, or characteristics appear connected or influence one another.
  • Visual Analysis. Represent information visually to make relationships, associations, and interactions easier to identify.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Cause-and-Effect Mapping
  • Correlation Analysis
  • Cross-Tabulation
  • Relationship Mapping
  • Scatter Plots
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Data Analysis Assistants & Code Interpreters (Julius AI, Claude Artifacts, ChatGPT Data Analysis)
  • Data Visualization Tools
  • Electronic Worksheets
  • Statistical Analysis Tools
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 6. I Am Not Sure Whether My Information is Trustworthy
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Different sources provide conflicting information.
  • Information comes from multiple sources of varying quality.
  • You are uncertain whether information is accurate, reliable, or credible.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Are there reasons to question the reliability of the source?
  • Can the information be verified?
  • Do multiple sources support the same claim?
  • Where did this information come from?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Credibility Assessment. Evaluate whether information appears reliable, accurate, and trustworthy.
  • Verification. Confirm information using additional evidence, sources, records, or observations.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • CRAAP Test
  • Cross-Verification
  • Lateral Reading
  • Source Evaluation
  • Source Triangulation
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Academic Search Engines (Elicit, Consensus)
  • Citation Analysis Tools (Scite.ai)
  • Fact-Checking Databases
  • Reference Management Tools
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 7. I Do Not Understand What an Observation May Mean
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Several possible explanations seem reasonable.
  • You identify a pattern but do not know what it suggests.
  • You notice a difference between groups but cannot explain it.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Does the available evidence support this interpretation?
  • What alternative interpretations should be considered?
  • What factors may help explain this result?
  • What may this observation suggest?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Alternative Perspectives. Explore multiple possible explanations before deciding which interpretation appears strongest.
  • Interpretation Development. Develop plausible explanations by examining observations within the broader context of the project.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Alternative Interpretation Development
  • Comparative Analysis
  • Contextual Analysis
  • Interpretation Questions
  • Ladder of Inference
  • Peer and/or Expert Consultation
Possible Tools
  • AI Socratic Prompting & Roleplaying Systems
  • Mind-Mapping Tools
  • Asynchronous Peer-Review & Discussion Boards (e.g., LMS Forums, Threaded Canvas/Moodle Discussions)
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 8. I Have Several Interpretations and Do Not Know Which Are Strongest
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• Different explanations seem equally convincing.
  • Multiple interpretations appear reasonable.
  • You are unsure which interpretation is best supported by evidence.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Does any interpretation contradict available evidence?
  • Have alternative explanations been considered fairly?
  • Which interpretation is most strongly supported by evidence?
  • Which interpretations depend on assumptions?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Alternative Explanation Analysis. Evaluate competing interpretations by comparing explanations and actively looking for weaknesses, contradictions, or counterexamples.
  • External Review. Seek feedback from knowledgeable individuals who may identify strengths, weaknesses, or assumptions that were overlooked.
  • Evidence-Based Validation. Determine which interpretation is best supported by the available evidence.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH)
  • Counterexample Testing
  • Evidence Mapping
  • Evidence Review
  • Interpretation Comparison
  • Peer and/or Expert Consultation
Possible Tools
  • AI Adversarial Prompting Systems
  • Argument Mapping Tools
  • Mind-Mapping Tools
Online Sources
  • [TBD]

docs.title: 9. I Am Not Sure Whether a Finding Is Actually Supported
This May Happen When
docs.text:
• A finding appears reasonable, but supporting evidence is unclear.
  • Multiple findings have been developed and require validation.
  • You are unsure whether a finding goes beyond the available information.

docs.title: Questions to Ask Yourself
docs.text:
• Am I claiming more than the evidence supports?
  • Could the evidence support a different finding?
  • Does the finding remain faithful to the original observation?
  • What evidence supports this finding?

docs.title: Possible Approaches
docs.text:
• Alternative Explanation Analysis. Evaluate whether alternative explanations could account for the same evidence.
  • Evidence-Based Validation. Determine whether a finding is directly supported by the available evidence.
  • Scope and Limitation Review. Evaluate whether a finding remains within the boundaries and limitations of the available information.
Support Frameworks & Techniques
  • Boundary Checking
  • Claim-Evidence Matrix
  • Counterexample Testing
  • Evidence Mapping
  • Finding Validation
  • Limitation Analysis
Possible Tools
  • AI-Powered Academic Search Engines (specifically for scientific consensus & counterexample verification, e.g., Elicit, Consensus)
  • Annotation & Evidence Tracking Tools
  • Claim–Evidence Matrix Tools (Notion, Airtable, Structured Tables)
Online Sources
